name: Northfork Mono, i.e. Western Mono / Monachi

catalog_quote: 107. Stress is an automatic feature of Northfork; its positions of occurrence are determined by configurations of consonants, vowels, and junctures. a. Except under the conditions stated in 107b,c, the position of stress is determined as follows: for words ending in /V/, the syllable which contains the next-to-last /V/ in thw word is stressed; for words ending in /C/, the last syllable is stressed. The occurrence of stress on syllables preceding the last stressed syllable of a word is determined in a similar manner: the syllable containing the second /V/ before the last stressed syllable of the word is stressed (if there is one); the syllable containing the second /V/ before such a stressed syllable is stressed; etc. Thus the incidence of stress on a given word may be predicted by counting backwards from the end of the word. b. If the first syllable of a word does not meet the above conditions for being stressed, nor those of 107c, it nevertheless has a weak degree of stress. ... [p. 24, on /VV/:] The vowel clusters which occur are: /ii yy uu ee aa oo yi ui ei ai oi/, and, in a single word (/ʔeaʔa/, an interjection), /ea/. That is, any vowel may be followed by itself or by /i/.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is non-phonemic and computed from the right edge of the word by counting vowels (moras, since /VV/ counts as two /V/): in a vowel-final word the syllable containing the penultimate /V/ is stressed (penult for CV-syllable words, but a final CVV syllable takes the stress), in a consonant-final word the last syllable is stressed; going leftward, the syllable containing every second /V/ before a stressed one is also stressed (a moraic right-to-left alternating pattern). Under narrow conditions (107c: three preceding light syllables, vowel identity, cluster conditions) a three-syllable stress unit occurs, but never at the end of the word. §101 (p. 19): 'there is a systematic stress pattern and a very elaborate intonational apparatus, although no stress phonemes nor phonemic pitch levels are necessary to describe the prosody'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Four degrees (§107d, p. 26): strong stress on the last stressed syllable before the juncture /./ (unless the suprasegmental phoneme /'/ of §161 occurs earlier); intermediate stress on every other syllable selected by 107a,c (i.e. the leftward alternating stresses); weak stress on an initial syllable that is not otherwise stressed (107b); all others unstressed. Stress units (§107e) of 1-3 syllables tend to equal duration (stress-timed rhythm, p. 27).
new_statements.exceptions: 107c: a three-syllable stress unit (stress on the third syllable before a stressed one) only when the three preceding syllables each contain a single /V/, the second-preceding vowel is identical to an adjoining vowel, and specified consonant-cluster conditions hold; examples /,suwah,kwinunu'hihti./ 'is dizzy'. No stress ever on the third syllable from the end with the intervening syllables unstressed. Suprasegmental phoneme /'/ (§161) can shift the strong stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonemic word (bounded by the word-juncture /+/); the description is of the Northfork subdialect (North Fork, Madera County) of Western Mono, based on one main speaker (Lucy Kinsman) from 1953-55 fieldwork; stress marked in examples though not phonemic. Sentence-level strong stress is defined relative to the juncture /./.
new_statements.identity_note: Lamb 1958 describes 'Northfork Mono', the Northfork subdialect of the San Joaquin (Western Mono) dialect, from North Fork, Madera County (intro pp. 15-16 and preface). Glottolog 5.x mono1275 is language-level with no dialect children, so no separate glottocode exists for Western vs. Eastern Mono (Owens Valley Paiute); the Eastern dialect is not covered by this statement (Norris 1986 would be the source).

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same source and same passage as the existing statement (Lamb 1958 §107, reading weight-sensitive). The quote is now verified verbatim against the page image (thesis p. 24 = PDF p. 25): the scanned's 'words endings' reads 'words ending' on the page; 'thw word' is a typo in the original typescript. The catalog record itself has an empty rule field; Lamb supplies the rule (penultimate vowel unit / final closed syllable, automatic, alternating leftward, four degrees, phrasal primary stress). Adds §107b-e detail (weak initial stress, 3-syllable exception, four degrees, stress-unit timing) beyond the existing statement's truncated §107a.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is automatic, not phonemic (§101 p. 19: 'there is a systematic stress pattern and a very elaborate intonational apparatus, although no stress phonemes nor phonemic pitch levels are necessary to describe the prosody'). Its position is counted in vowel units (morae) from the right edge of the word: a word ending in a vowel stresses the syllable that contains the next-to-last /V/ (so the penult when the last syllable has a single short vowel, but the final syllable when it contains a /VV/ sequence, e.g. /maiwai/ 'will be'); a word ending in a consonant stresses its last syllable. Long vowels and diphthongs (/VV/) count as two units, so stress placement depends on syllable weight; the pattern amounts to 'stress the syllable containing the penultimate mora'. Continuing leftward, every second /V/ before a stressed syllable is stressed (alternating rhythm), giving one- to three-syllable 'stress units' of roughly equal duration (§107e, pp. 26-27). Strong (primary) stress is phrasal: it falls on the last stressed syllable before the juncture /./ unless the suprasegmental phoneme /'/ (§161) occurs on a preceding syllable (§107d, p. 26).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: §107a continues 'the syllable containing the second /V/ before such a stressed syllable is stressed; etc. Thus the incidence of stress on a given word may be predicted by counting backwards from the end of the word' (p. 24-25). §107d (p. 26): 'There are four degrees of stress. Strong stress occurs on the last stressed syllable before /./, unless the suprasegmental phoneme /'/ (161) occurs on a preceding syllable; and with /'/. Intermediate stress occurs on any other syllable which is determined as stressed by the conditions of 107a,c. Weak stress (unmarked in the examples above) occurs on initial syllables which do not meet the conditions of 107a,c for being stressed (107b). Any other syllable is unstressed.' §107b (p. 25): an initial syllable that would otherwise be unstressed 'nevertheless has a weak degree of stress.'
new_statements.exceptions: §107c (p. 25): 'Under certain conditions, stress may occur on the third syllable preceding a stressed syllable, with the intervening two syllables unstressed.. There are no occurrences, however, of stress on the third syllable from the end of a word, with the intervening syllables unstressed.' The four conditions are segmental: each of the three syllables must contain a single /V/ (not /VV/), the vowel of the second preceding syllable must be identical to an adjoining vowel, the /C/ before the second preceding /V/ must be preceded by /V/ (not /C/), and the /C/ before the third preceding /V/ must be preceded by /C/ or /#/. Examples pp. 25-26, e.g. /,suwah,kwinunu'hihti./ 'is dizzy', /pu,hitu'wahpy./ 'has become green' vs. not */,puhitu'wahpy./. Also §107e: stress units of 1-3 syllables tend to equal duration ('a /VV/ sequence is longer in a CVV stress unit than in a CVVCV one'), i.e. stress-timed rhythm.
new_statements.identity_note: Lamb 1958 describes the Northfork subdialect of the San Joaquin (Western) dialect of Mono/Monachi, based on the speech of Lucy Kinsman (North Fork, Madera County, fieldwork 1953-55), with occasional comments on other speakers (Introduction §2-3, pp. 13-14: 'the structure here described can be assumed to be adequately representative of the Northfork subdialect of Mono'). Lamb notes in passing (p. 29) that other Mono dialects differ segmentally (e.g. /s/ after vowels). This is Western Mono = Glottolog mono1275 [mnr], not Eastern Mono (Owens Valley Paiute), which is a separate Glottolog language.
